claims.text: Adding boron or carbon to a eutectic high-entropy alloy can simultaneously improve its strength and ductility.
The proposed intervention applies to structural applications at elevated temperatures.
The minor additions refine the alloy's grain structure.
The minor additions promote precipitation hardening.
Grain refinement and precipitation hardening lead to improved strength.
Grain refinement and precipitation hardening lead to improved ductility.
The intervention will increase yield strength by at least 15% relative to the alloy without the addition.
The intervention will increase elongation at break by at least 20% relative to the alloy without the addition.
The appropriate baseline is the corresponding alloy composition without the added boron or carbon.
The intervention is expected to be effective when the added element constitutes 10–20% of the alloy.
The intervention is expected to be effective between 500 and 700°C.
Other alloying elements may affect the response to the intervention.
The temperature dependence of the proposed grain-refinement and precipitation-hardening mechanisms is uncertain.
A tensile test at 600°C on an alloy containing 15% boron can test the hypothesis.
A yield strength below 1000 MPa or elongation at break below 15% in that test would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes the additions as minor, but the stated range is 10–20% and the test uses 15% boron, which is not clearly consistent with a minor addition.

The predicted improvements are relative percentages versus an unmodified baseline, whereas the falsification rule uses absolute thresholds without measuring the baseline; these criteria can therefore yield inconsistent conclusions.
